claims.claim: The CPU processes instructions by repeating a fetch-decode-execute cycle: it fetches the next instruction from memory, decodes it, executes it, and repeats.

Clock speed is measured in hertz (cycles per second); modern CPUs are rated in gigahertz (GHz), so a 3 GHz processor runs on the order of three billion cycles per second, and many CPUs contain multiple cores.
RAM is volatile: it holds its contents only while powered, so data in RAM is lost at shutdown or on power loss. Storage is non-volatile: it retains data without power.

Computer memory is organized as a hierarchy - CPU registers and cache, then RAM, then storage - in which higher levels are faster, smaller, and more expensive per byte, and lower levels are slower, larger, and cheaper.
A bit is a single binary digit (0 or 1) and eight bits make one byte; larger capacities are expressed in kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes, and terabytes.

Decimal (SI) prefixes are powers of 1,000 (1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes) while IEC binary prefixes are powers of 1,024 (1 MiB = 2^20 = 1,048,576 bytes; 1 GiB = 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 bytes), which is why a labeled drive can appear to hold slightly less once formatted.

A hard disk drive (HDD) stores data magnetically on spinning platters read by a moving arm, whereas a solid-state drive (SSD) stores data in NAND flash memory with no moving parts, making SSDs faster and more durable; both are non-volatile.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'kilobyte/megabyte/gigabyte' mean powers of 1,000 or powers of 1,024
positions: Storage manufacturers and the SI convention use decimal powers of 1,000
Operating systems and older usage often report binary powers of 1,024, which the IEC names kibibyte/mebibyte/gibibyte
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both conventions are in use. The lesson explains the difference and uses the IEC binary-prefix names for the powers-of-1,024 quantities, following NIST/IEC guidance, and notes this is why formatted capacity looks smaller than the label.

sourceRecords.title: Prefixes for Binary Multiples
sourceRecords.provider: NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative source for information units. States 1 kbit = 10^3 bits vs 1 Kibit = 2^10 = 1,024 bits; 1 MB = 10^6 B vs 1 MiB = 2^20 = 1,048,576 B; 1 GB = 10^9 B vs 1 GiB = 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 B, and that the IEC binary prefixes (IEC 60027-2, Amendment 2, 1999) are not part of the SI. Supports the bit/byte and decimal-vs-binary-prefix claims.
